Key Takeaway: Global homicide rates have generally declined over the past three decades, with the median rate falling from 3.4 per 100,000 in 1990 to 1.8 in 2023. However, significant disparities persist across regions, genders, and age groups. Males face homicide rates approximately 2.6 times higher than females, and the Americas region consistently records the highest rates.

1. Global Homicide Rate Overview

This analysis draws on 22,092 observations spanning 201 countries and territories across 34 distinct years (1990–2023). The dataset is an unbalanced panel — the number of countries reporting homicide data varies substantially from year to year, which directly impacts aggregated statistics.

Figure 1: Global median and mean homicide rates over time. The grey bars indicate the number of countries reporting each year. The gap between mean and median reflects the right-skewed distribution driven by high-rate outlier nations.

The global median homicide rate provides a more robust measure of central tendency than the mean, as it is less sensitive to extreme values from a small number of high-homicide nations. As shown in Figure 1, both the median and mean rates have generally trended downward since the early 2000s, though reporting coverage has fluctuated — rising from fewer countries in the 1990s to broader participation in recent years.

The persistent gap between mean and median rates underscores the asymmetric nature of global homicide — a relatively small number of countries with very high rates pull the global average upward, while the majority of nations maintain rates well below this average.

Decade-over-Decade Trajectory

Comparing decade averages provides a smoothed view of long-term trends:

  • 2000s average (mean): 8.51 per 100,000
  • 2010s average (mean): 7.70 per 100,000 (-9.6% vs 2000s)
  • 2020s average (mean): 7.71 per 100,000 (+0.2% vs 2010s)

2. Regional & Country-Level Comparison

Regional groupings reveal stark geographic patterns in homicide rates. The Americas consistently record the highest median rates, driven by persistently elevated homicide levels in parts of Central America, the Caribbean, and South America. Europe and Asia maintain substantially lower rates, while Africa shows considerable within-region variation due to uneven data reporting.

Figure 2: Median homicide rate by world region over time. The Americas and Africa consistently outpace other regions, while Europe shows a sustained downward trend.

3. Gender Disparity in Homicide Victimization

Critical Finding: Globally, males are approximately 2.6 times more likely to be victims of intentional homicide than females. This ratio has remained persistently high throughout the observation period, representing one of the most consistent demographic disparities in violent death worldwide.

Gender-disaggregated data reveals a profound and persistent disparity in homicide victimization. Across virtually every country and year in the dataset, male homicide rates substantially exceed female rates. This pattern holds across all regions, though the absolute magnitude and ratio vary by geography.

Figure 4: Top panel — median homicide rates for males and females over time, with the shaded area representing the gap. Bottom panel — the male-to-female rate ratio over time.

The male-to-female ratio has fluctuated over the observation period, but has consistently remained well above 1.0. The average ratio across all years with sex-disaggregated data is approximately 3.2×. This disparity reflects the disproportionate involvement of males in both perpetrating and becoming victims of lethal violence.

Gender Disparity by Region

Figure 5: Male vs. female median homicide rates by region, with the male-to-female ratio displayed above each male bar. The Americas show both the highest absolute rates and a substantial gender gap.

The regional breakdown confirms that the gender gap is a global phenomenon, not confined to any single region. However, regions with higher overall homicide rates tend to exhibit larger absolute differences between male and female rates, even when the ratio is similar. This suggests that escalating violence disproportionately affects males.

4. Age Group Analysis

Age-disaggregated data, while less uniformly reported than sex-disaggregated data, reveals important patterns in who is most at risk. The age group 25-29 shows the highest median homicide rate at 3.1 per 100,000, confirming that young adults bear a disproportionate burden of lethal violence.

Figure 6: Median homicide rate by age group across all available data. Young adults (15–29 and 30–44) face the highest risk.

Age and Sex Interaction

When age and sex are considered jointly, the pattern sharpens dramatically. Young males (15–29) face the single highest homicide risk of any demographic group, reflecting their overrepresentation in situations of interpersonal and gang-related violence.

Figure 7: Homicide rates by age group and sex. The male-female disparity is most pronounced in the 15–29 and 30–44 age brackets.

Children (0–14) consistently show the lowest homicide rates across both sexes, while the elderly (60+) exhibit moderate rates with a less pronounced gender gap compared to younger cohorts. The peak risk period for males — ages 15 to 44 — corresponds with the age range most associated with gang involvement, interpersonal conflict, and organized crime victimization in the criminological literature.

Spotlight: Selected Country Trajectories

Figure 9: Homicide rate trajectories for selected high-profile countries, illustrating diverse experiences from dramatic declines (Colombia) to relative stability (Japan).

Colombia stands out as a major success story, with homicide rates declining dramatically from some of the highest in the world in the 1990s. Conversely, Mexico has experienced a notable uptick in homicide rates since the late 2000s. Japan and several other Asian and European nations consistently maintain among the lowest rates globally.

6. Data Limitations & Policy Recommendations

Data Limitations

Figure 10: Number of countries reporting homicide data each year. Fluctuations in reporting coverage directly affect the comparability of year-over-year statistics.

Key Caveats

  • Unbalanced panel: Not all countries report in all years. The set of reporting countries changes annually, meaning that shifts in aggregated statistics may partly reflect changes in the composition of reporters rather than genuine trends.
  • Reporting gaps: Some countries have only a handful of observations while others have near-complete time series. Year-over-year comparisons for individual countries should account for potential gaps.
  • United Kingdom: UK data refer to England and Wales only, as reported in the original UNODC dataset. Scotland and Northern Ireland are reported separately.
  • Territories: Some territories (e.g., Hong Kong, Puerto Rico) appear as distinct entries and should not be double-counted with parent countries in national aggregations.
  • No imputation: Missing values were not interpolated or imputed. All figures in this report derive directly from observed data points.
  • Age and sex disaggregation: Demographic breakdowns are less consistently reported than overall rates. The set of countries contributing to age- and sex-specific analyses is smaller and may not be globally representative.
  • Reporting accuracy: Homicide statistics depend on national law enforcement and vital registration systems, which vary in completeness and methodology across countries. Under-reporting is a concern, particularly in conflict-affected and low-capacity settings.

Policy Recommendations

For Policy Analysts: The following recommendations are derived directly from the patterns observed in the data. They are intended to inform resource allocation and intervention design, not to prescribe specific policies.
  1. Prioritize the Americas and Africa for violence reduction investments. These regions consistently exhibit the highest homicide rates. Targeted interventions addressing root causes — organized crime, socioeconomic inequality, and weak rule of law — are critical.
  2. Address the male victimization crisis. With males facing homicide rates 2.6× higher than females, programs targeting young men (ages 15–44) should be a priority. This includes community violence intervention programs, employment initiatives, and conflict mediation services.
  3. Invest in youth-focused prevention. The 15–29 age group faces the highest homicide risk. Early intervention programs, educational access, and alternative livelihood pathways can address root vulnerabilities before they escalate.
  4. Strengthen data infrastructure. The uneven reporting coverage highlighted in this analysis limits the ability to track progress globally. Investment in national statistical capacity, particularly in Africa and parts of Asia, is essential for evidence-based policymaking.
  5. Learn from success cases. Countries like Colombia that have achieved dramatic reductions in homicide rates offer valuable lessons in integrated security strategies, institutional reform, and community-based approaches that other high-rate nations could adapt.
  6. Monitor emerging deteriorations. Several countries show worsening trends that warrant early attention. Proactive engagement before rates escalate further is more cost-effective than reactive crisis response.

Methodology Note

Data Source: UNODC Crime Trends Survey (CTS) via Kaggle (lucalullo/global-homicide-rates-by-country). All rates are expressed as victims of intentional homicide per 100,000 population.

Analysis Period: 1990–2023 | Total Observations: 22,092 | Countries/Territories: 201 | Years Covered: 34

Regional Classification: Countries are grouped into five macro regions (Africa, Americas, Asia, Europe, Oceania) based on UN geographic classification using ISO 3166-1 alpha-3 codes.

Aggregation: Median values are used as the primary measure of central tendency to mitigate the influence of outlier nations. Mean values are provided for context. All statistics are computed from the raw data without imputation.

Filtering: Country-level comparisons use sex='both' and age_group='ALL'. Gender analysis uses sex='male' or sex='female' with age_group='ALL'. Age analysis uses specific age groups.
